limitations: The evidence is mostly project policy documents and maintainer statements. They show stated burden and motivation, not measured PR volumes or time costs.
Selection bias: projects that wrote policies are those most affected. Projects reporting no problem are under-represented.
No quantitative data on volumes or acceptance rates was retrieved, and no figures are claimed.
Competitor scan limited to GitHub repository search; commercial products (e.g. code-review vendors, bug-bounty platform triage) were not examined.
GitHub's newer PR-management features that news reports mention couldn't be verified beyond the docs pages retrieved.

limitations: Evidence comes from arXiv abstracts only. Full papers, methods and datasets weren't examined.
Most studies use the AIDev dataset of agent-authored PRs, which differs from unsolicited inbound contributions to popular projects.
HN leads such as 'Linux Foundation Estimates 25% of New Pull Requests to Be Low-Quality AI Slop' were only titles in the signal feed. They weren't used as evidence and still need primary sources.

The evidence-strength formula changed during this run: contradictions aimed at an idea now count double. Snapshots from the first run use the earlier formula, so part of the detector's drop (61 → 50) comes from the method change, not new evidence.
